region: Europe, North Africa and western Asia; widely planted in gardens and churchyards
description: Yew is a dense, fine-grained softwood with orange-brown heartwood and creamy sapwood. Woodworkers use it for turning, carving, cabinet work and traditional longbows.

hazards.summary: Swallowing yew needles (leaves), and less often other parts of the plant, can cause life-threatening heart rhythm problems and has caused deaths; the toxic taxine alkaloids have been measured in patients' blood. This evidence is about eating the plant, not about woodworking dust.

The UK HSE lists headache, a fall in blood pressure and heart effects among reported effects of working yew. We found no primary case report of heart problems from yew wood dust, so how much toxin the dust delivers is unknown.
The UK HSE lists dermatitis from yew. It does not say whether this is irritation or allergy, and no primary report was found.
All wood dust is classified as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancers of the nose and sinuses. This applies to this wood like every other species.

known_compounds.name: taxine B
known_compounds.role: Most potent cardiotoxic yew alkaloid in isolated heart experiments; slows heart conduction

known_compounds.name: taxine alkaloids
known_compounds.role: Block sodium and calcium currents in heart muscle cells

related_species_note: Other yews (e.g. Pacific yew Taxus brevifolia, Japanese yew Taxus cuspidata) also contain taxine alkaloids; this entry's evidence is from Taxus baccata.
image_prompt: Photorealistic studio photograph of a freshly planed English yew (Taxus baccata) board, shot at a low three-quarter angle so the face grain fills most of the frame. Rich orange-brown to reddish-amber heartwood with a sharply contrasting band of creamy white sapwood along one edge. Very fine, dense texture with tight, slightly wavy growth rings, small pin knots and occasional burl-like swirls, a natural lustrous sheen, and no visible pores. Soft diffused daylight from upper left, gentle falloff, neutral warm-grey seamless background, shallow depth of field with the near edge tack-sharp. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.

notes_internal: Botanical name verified on WFO (Taxus baccata L., Taxaceae). The ingestion cardiac hazard is very well documented (case series with taxines measured in serum, ECG findings, fatalities) but is set at level 3 because our scale's level 1 criteria are for sensitization tests; reviewer may want a different label. Ingestion evidence checked is mainly leaves (Grobosch) plus pulp, bark and tea (Reijnen). Seed toxicity is widely stated but no primary seed paper was read; 'seeds' is not in the source_part enum anyway. Dust-route systemic/cardiac and dermatitis rest on HSE-WIS30 only; no primary woodworker case found in PubMed. Wilson-2001 (Tier B review) defined for background only.
